'''Rosa Margaret Morris''' (16 July 1914 – 15 October 2011)<ref name="obit">{{Cite news |date=2011-10-27 |title=R Morris |language=en |work=South Wales Argus |url=https://www.southwalesargus.co.uk/announcements/deaths/deaths/9329491.R_MORRIS/ |access-date=2021-03-06}}</ref> was a Welsh applied mathematician, working in [[potential theory]] and [[aerodynamics]]. When she was 23, her research and examination results made national and international news. She received several fellowships and awards before graduating with a PhD in mathematics from the University of Cambridge in 1940. In her later career, she taught at the University College of South Wales and Monmouthshire (now [[Cardiff University]]), where she co-authored a successful textbook on ''Mathematical Methods of Physics'' with [[John Stephen Roy Chisholm|Roy Chisholm]] and became one of the first female Heads of School of Mathematics in the United Kingdom.

== Early life and education ==
Morris was born in [[Rogerstone]], [[Monmouthshire (historic)|Monmouthshire]],<ref name="obit"/> the youngest child of John and Mary Aline Morris, {{nee|Roberts}}. Her father, who died when she was young, was the headmaster of the elementary school in Rogerstone,<ref name="risca">{{Cite magazine |last=Osment |first=Bernard |date=May–June 2019 |title=Renowned Mathematician |url=http://sw-directories.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/Risca.pdf |magazine=Risca Directory |page=12 |access-date=2025-02-02 |archive-date=2025-02-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250202152718/http://sw-directories.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/Risca.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="girton">{{Cite book |last=Girton College (University of Cambridge) |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mIefAAAAMAAJ&q=rosa+margaret+morris+1914 |title=Girton College Register: 1869–1946 |date=1948 |publisher=Privately printed for Girton College |pages=549 |language=en |access-date=10 March 2021 |archive-date=19 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419085234/https://books.google.com/books?id=mIefAAAAMAAJ&newbks=0&printsec=frontcover&dq=rosa+margaret+morris+1914&q=rosa+margaret+morris+1914&hl=en |url-status=live }}</ref> and her mother was a schoolmistress.<ref name="times">{{Cite news |date=1938-07-28 |title=A Mathematical Genius |language=English |pages=16 |work=The Times |issn=0140-0460 |url=https://link.gale.com/apps/doc/CS270873340/TTDA?u=wikipedia&sid=TTDA&xid=2bbd6492 |access-date=9 April 2021 |archive-date=19 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419085235/https://go.gale.com/ps/i.do?p=TTDA&u=wikipedia&id=GALE{{!}}CS270873340&v=2.1&it=r&sid=TTDA&asid=2bbd6492 |url-status=live }}</ref> Morris first attended Rogerstone School, then Pontywaun County School, [[Pontymister]], [[Risca]],<ref name="wigmore">{{Cite news |last=Wigmore |first=Sarah |date=2023-06-25 |title=Look: When closure of school by 'little dictators' sparked a protest |url=https://www.southwalesargus.co.uk/news/23605654.looking-back-pontywaun-grammar-school-risca/ |access-date=2025-02-02 |work=South Wales Argus |language=en}}</ref><ref name="girton" /> from 1926 to 1932, with Distinctions in Pure and Applied Mathematics.<ref name="risca"/> She studied mathematics at the [[University College of South Wales and Monmouthshire]] (now Cardiff University) in [[Cardiff]], graduating with a first class degree in 1936 and continuing as a research student until 1938,<ref name="girton"/> working under the supervision of [[George Henry Livens]].<ref name="diss">{{Cite thesis |last=Morris |first=Rosa Margaret |title=Two-dimensional potential theory, with special reference to aerodynamic problems |date=1940 |degree=PhD |publisher=Cambridge University|url=https://idiscover.lib.cam.ac.uk/permalink/f/t9gok8/44CAM_ALMA21668394560003606}}</ref>

During this time, Morris, aged 23, published her first articles, on potential theory<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Morris |first=Rosa M. |date=October 1937 |title=Two-Dimensional Potential Problems |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0305004100077616/type/journal_article |journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]] |language=en |volume=33 |issue=4 |pages=474–484 |doi=10.1017/S0305004100077616 |bibcode=1937PCPS...33..474M |s2cid=120558044 |issn=0305-0041|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and aerodynamics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Morris |first=Rosa M. |date=1937-08-03 |title=The two-dimensional hydrodynamical theory of moving aerofoils—I |journal= Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Mathematical and Physical Sciences|volume=161 |issue=906 |pages=406–419 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1937.0152 |bibcode=1937RSPSA.161..406M |doi-access=free }}</ref> Her approach showed "the advantages of using the complex variable in ... boundary problems of [[mathematical physics]]"<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Stevenson |first=A. C. |date=1938 |title=Flexure with Shear and Associated Torsion in Prisms of Uni-Axial and Asymmetric Cross-Sections |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/91357 |journal= Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Mathematical and Physical Sciences|volume=237 |issue=776 |page=181 <!-- |pages=161–229 --> |jstor=91357 |issn=0080-4614}}</ref> and made national news with [[human interest]] stories focusing on her as a "mathematical genius", having "found a method of solving problems in aerodynamics which have hitherto defied all mathematicians". She was described as a "keen [[field hockey|hockey]] player and accomplished dressmaker", and University College of South Wales and Monmouthshire Principal [[Frederick Rees]] stated that at her examination, she would have been entitled to 130 percent compared to the next best student, and a special case had to be made for her to avoid handicapping other students.<ref name="times"/><ref name="bjn">{{Cite journal |date=August 1938 |title=A Mathematical Genius |url=https://rcnarchive.rcn.org.uk/data/VOLUME086-1938/page221-volume86-august1938.pdf |journal=[[The British Journal of Nursing]] |volume=86 |pages=221 |access-date=6 March 2021 |archive-date=19 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419085238/https://rcnarchive.rcn.org.uk/data/VOLUME086-1938/page221-volume86-august1938.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="NUWT">{{Cite magazine |magazine=The Woman Teacher|last=<!-- no byline --> |date=1938-09-30 |title=A Woman's Triumph in Aero-Dynamics |url=https://jstor.org/stable/community.28299230 |page=383 |access-date=6 April 2021 |archive-date=19 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419085312/https://www.jstor.org/stable/community.28299230 |url-status=live }}</ref> Short reports on her achievements were also printed in American local newspapers.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1938-09-04 |title=The Paris News from Paris, Texas |language=en |page=28 |work=The Paris News |location=Paris, Texas |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/7933558/ |access-date=2021-04-06}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=1938-08-30 |title=Lead Daily Call from Lead, South Dakota |page=4 |language=en |url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/93913148/ |access-date=2021-04-06 |archive-date=19 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419085249/https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/93913148/ |url-status=live }}</ref> 

Morris won scholarships worth £600 for the first year at [[Girton College, Cambridge]],<ref name="times"/><ref name="bjn" /> where she was a [[Margaret Meyer|M. T. Meyer]] research student.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1938-07-02 |title=University News |language=English |pages=[18] |work=The Daily Telegraph |url=https://link.gale.com/apps/doc/IO0708413053/TGRH?u=univnott&sid=zotero&xid=62d92897 |access-date=2021-04-06 |issn=0307-1235 |archive-date=19 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419085309/https://go.gale.com/ps/i.do?p=TGRH&u=univnott&id=GALE{{!}}IO0708413053&v=2.1&it=r&sid=zotero&asid=62d92897 |url-status=live }}</ref> Her fellowships and awards included a University of Wales Fellowship (1938–1940) and a [[Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (United Kingdom)|Department of Scientific and Industrial Research]] Senior Research Award (1939–1941).<ref name="girton"/> After three years as a research student, one of them in Cardiff, two in Cambridge,<ref name="diss"/> she obtained her PhD from [[Cambridge University]] in 1940, with the thesis ''Two-dimensional potential theory, with special reference to aerodynamic problems.''<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cambridge |first=University of |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=I4wcAAAAMAAJ&q=morris |title=Abstracts of Dissertations Approved for the Ph.D., M.Sc., and M.Litt. Degrees in the University of Cambridge |date=1941 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |language=en |access-date=7 April 2021 |archive-date=19 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419085249/https://books.google.co.uk/books?newbks=0&redir_esc=y&id=I4wcAAAAMAAJ&focus=searchwithinvolume&q=morris |url-status=live }}</ref> Her Cambridge advisor was [[Geoffrey Ingram Taylor]].<ref name="diss"/><ref>{{Cite journal |date=1940-03-12 |title=Annual Report of the Board of Research Studies|last=Board of Research Studies |journal=[[Cambridge University Reporter]] |publisher=Cambridge University |volume=LXX No.26 |issue=3239 |page=631}}
</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Rosa M. Morris |url=https://www.mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=67329 |website=[[Mathematics Genealogy Project]] |access-date=5 April 2021 |archive-date=3 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200703063002/https://mathgenealogy.org/id.php?id=67329 |url-status=live }}</ref> Perhaps to save her family money, Morris went to Cambridge by bike.<ref name="jones" />

== Professional career ==
Morris graduated with a PhD in 1940 and became a faculty member in Cardiff in 1941,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Morris, Rosa |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Davis/Names/Morris_Rosa_.html |access-date=2021-04-05 |website=[[mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk]] |archive-date=19 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210419085251/https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Davis/Names/Morris_Rosa_.html |url-status=live }}</ref> where she stayed for the rest of her career. She supervised the 1955 PhD thesis of [[David Edmunds]], who later won the [[Pólya Prize (LMS)|Pólya Prize]].<ref>{{Cite book |title=Spectral theory, function spaces and inequalities : new techniques and recent trends |date=2012 |isbn=978-3-0348-0263-5 |publisher=Birkhäuser |location=Basel |pages=ix-x |chapter=David Edmunds’ Mathematical Work |oclc=761201127|last1=Malcolm Brown |first1=B. |last2=Lang |first2=Jan |last3=Wood |first3=Ian G. }}</ref> Together with [[John Stephen Roy Chisholm|Roy Chisholm]], Morris wrote a textbook titled ''Mathematical Methods in Physics''.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Chisholm |first1=John Stephen Roy |title=Mathematical methods in physics |last2=Morris |first2=Rosa M |date=1964 |publisher=North-Holland |location=Amsterdam |language=English |oclc=610944321}}</ref> It was lacking in rigour,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mullin |first1=A. A. |date=1966-01-01 |title=Mathematical Methods in Physics. J. S. R. Chisholm and R. M. Morris |url=https://aapt.scitation.org/doi/10.1119/1.1972796 |journal=American Journal of Physics |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=79 |doi=10.1119/1.1972796 |issn=0002-9505 |access-date=5 April 2021 |archive-date=1 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180101053412/http://aapt.scitation.org/doi/10.1119/1.1972796 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and the reviewer for ''[[Mathematics of Computation]]'' called the mathematical content "not always adequate, and sometimes ... incorrect", giving as an example an untrue claim about the [[convergence of Fourier series]] for a [[continuous function]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=S. |first=D. |date=1966 |title=Review of Mathematical Methods in Physics |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2004316 |journal=Mathematics of Computation |volume=20 |issue=93 |pages=188–189 |doi=10.2307/2004316 |jstor=2004316 |s2cid=123322185 |issn=0025-5718|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Commercially, the book was a success and was reprinted several times. According to Chisholm, "in the late 1960's, North-Holland told us that we had broken their publication record for technical books. We even made a little money."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chisholm |first=Roy |title=Cardiff 1954 – 62 |url=http://roychisholm.com/cardiff-1954---62.html |access-date=2021-04-05 |website=Roy Chisholm |language=en |archive-date=27 January 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190127215240/http://www.roychisholm.com/cardiff-1954---62.html |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1972–1973, while Morris was a Reader in Fluid Dynamics, she served as one of the first female heads of a mathematics department in the UK, possibly the first at a university.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hobbs |first=Cathy |author-link=Catherine Hobbs |date=July 2015 |title=The first female head of department of mathematical sciences? |url=https://www.lms.ac.uk/sites/lms.ac.uk/files/files/July%202015.pdf |journal=Newsletter of the London Mathematical Society |issue=449 |pages=21–22 |access-date=9 March 2021 |archive-date=24 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210124070603/https://www.lms.ac.uk/sites/lms.ac.uk/files/files/July%202015.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=History of Mathematics at Cardiff |url=https://www.cardiff.ac.uk/mathematics/about-us/history-of-mathematics-at-cardiff |access-date=2022-07-06 |website=Cardiff University |language=en}}</ref> Morris retired in 1975.<ref name="jones" />

Morris was a member of the [[London Mathematical Society]] (since 1945),<ref>{{Cite book |last=Society |first=London Mathematical |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ofLuAAAAMAAJ |title=List of Members |year=1976 |pages=32 |language=en}}</ref> of the [[Mathematical Association]], where she was President of the Cardiff Branch 1955–1956,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Williams |first=W. H. |date=1956 |title=Report of the Cardiff Branch, 1955–56 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3609719 |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |volume=40 |issue=332 |pages=iii–iv |doi=10.1017/S0025557200222171 |jstor=3609719 |s2cid=185054236 |issn=0025-5572}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Williams |first=W. H. |date=1957 |title=Cardiff Branch: Report for the Session 1956-1957 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3609240 |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |volume=41 |issue=337 |pages=xix |doi=10.1017/S0025557200037128 |jstor=3609240 |s2cid=184617261 |issn=0025-5572}}</ref> and a Fellow of the [[Cambridge Philosophical Society]] until 1983.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=November 1984 |title=Proceedings of the meetings held during the session 1983–1984 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-proceedings-of-the-cambridge-philosophical-society/article/abs/proceedings-of-the-meetings-held-during-the-session-19831984/63303D28ADCE751BF2422A561085C2FE |journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]] |language=en |volume=96 |issue=3 |pages=555–563 |doi=10.1017/S0305004100062496 |bibcode=1984MPCPS..96..555. |s2cid=251092322 |issn=1469-8064|url-access=subscription }}</ref> She was a prolific contributor to ''[[Mathematical Reviews]]'', with 188 contributions credited to her name.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Items reviewed by Morris, Rosa M. |url=https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/search/publications.html?pg1=RVRI&s1=504039&pg3=authreviews |access-date=2021-04-06 |website=mathscinet.ams.org|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Personal life and legacy ==
[[File:Bethesda Baptist Chapel - geograph.org.uk - 5387323.jpg|thumb|Bethesda Baptist Church, Rogerstone]]
Morris was a life-long member of the congregation at Bethesda Baptist Church in Rogerstone.<ref name="jones">{{Cite magazine |last=Jones |first=Elin |date=March 2024 |title=Dr Rosa Morris: the first woman head of a university mathematics department? |url=https://www.womensarchivewales.org/getfile/newsletters/2024/newsletter-june-2024.pdf |access-date=2025-02-02 |magazine=Women's Archive Wales Newsletter |page=3 |volume=2024 |issue=June}}</ref> When she returned to Wales after completing her PhD studies in Cambridge, she lived in Rogerstone again, where she was a carer for her sister Olwen.<ref name="jones" /> After her 2011 death, Morris was buried in the churchyard of Bethesda church,<ref name="obit" /> in the same grave as her sister.<ref name="jones" /> The headstone describes her as a "renowned mathematician".<ref name="risca" /><ref name="jones" /> In local newspapers, her mathematical research is connected to the [[Supermarine Spitfire]] fighter aircraft.<ref name="wigmore" /><ref name="risca" />

Morris is listed in the Davis archive of about 2500 women who achieved honours degrees in Mathematics in Britain before 1940.<ref name="aldrich">{{Cite journal |last=Aldrich |first=John |date=2021-09-02 |title=Mathematical women in the British Isles 1878–1940: using the Davis archive |journal=British Journal for the History of Mathematics |volume=36 |issue=3 |pages=210–218 |doi=10.1080/26375451.2021.2003657 |issn=2637-5451|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="davis">{{Cite web |last=Davis |first=A E L |title=Davis archive index |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Davis/info.html |access-date=2025-02-02 |website=mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk}}</ref> The PhD was still an uncommon degree for British mathematicians at the time, and Morris is among only seven women who received Mathematics PhD degrees in Britain until 1940, and one of two from Cambridge.<ref name="aldrich" />

== Publications ==
Morris published research articles on [[potential theory]], [[fluid dynamics]] (especially moving aerofoils), and mathematical [[elasticity theory]].
